title: Distant opposition
summary: King and pawn against king: the opposition from afar and along the diagonal, and how to turn it into direct opposition.
part.distant.title: Distant opposition
part.distant.summary: With the kings far apart, the opposition is taken from afar and then turned into direct opposition.
part.diagonal.title: Along the diagonal, and in defence
part.diagonal.summary: The opposition also works along a diagonal, and it serves the defender too.
part.capablanca.title: Capablanca's example
part.capablanca.summary: Locked pawns and distant kings: whoever takes the opposition wins. And the opposition is a means, not an end.
step.t_lesson: The key squares of the g3 pawn are far from both kings. Think: if the white king runs straight for them, does the black king get there first? What is the right first step?
step.t_lesson.hint1: Put the kings on the same file and count the squares between them.
step.intro: You already know direct opposition: kings face to face, one square between them, and the other side to move. Here it is out of reach. My king is on d3, the black king on e8, and the key squares of the g3-pawn are f5, g5 and h5. If I just run there, the black king arrives first and stands in front. What decides this position is opposition at a distance: Ke4, on the same file as the black king.
step.odd: After Ke4 the kings are on the same file with three squares between them, e5, e6 and e7, and Black is to move. That is distant opposition. The rule is the rule of the odd number: kings on the same line, one, three or five squares between them, and the other side to move, you have the opposition. Capablanca put it the other way round: with an even number of squares, the player to move takes the opposition. By itself it is worth little. What it guarantees is that, with every step the black king takes, you can shorten the distance and reach direct opposition.
step.convert: White to play and win. Take the distant opposition and, with every move of the black king, bring yours closer until you have direct opposition and the key square.
step.convert.hint: Ke4 first, on the black king's file. Then, when he leaves the file, follow him: stand in front of him with one square in between.
step.convert.done: That's it. Ke4 from afar, Kf5 face to face, Kg5 on the key square. The black king gave up a step with every move, and the pawn queens.
step.t_diagonal: The black king guards the key squares of the e3 pawn. The white king's most natural move looks good. Is it? Look for the square that leaves the black king without a good answer.
step.t_diagonal.hint1: The kings need not be on the same file: a diagonal works too, with one square between them.
step.diagonal: Opposition exists along the diagonal too: kings on the same diagonal, one square between them, the other side to move. Here my king is on f3, the black king on d6. Ke4 looks natural, but after ...Ke6 it is the black king that has direct opposition, and the e3-pawn does not get through. The way in is Kf4: the diagonal f4, e5, d6. Now Black is the one who has to move, and wherever the black king steps, mine enters his file with direct opposition.
step.diagonalMove: White to play and win. Come in along the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and go to a key square of the e3-pawn.
step.diagonalMove.hint: Kf4, on the black king's diagonal. If he goes to e6, face him on e4. Then, when he gives way, jump to a key square: d5, e5 or f5.
step.diagonalMove.done: Very good. Kf4 along the diagonal, Ke4 face to face, and the king enters a key square (f5 is the free key square; Kd4 and Kf4 also win, preparing the entry). With the king on a key square, the pawn queens by itself.
step.means: A warning before we go on. The opposition is a means, not an end. In this position, Ke4 takes direct opposition and only draws: the black king answers ...Kd6, and you do not get through. Kc5 ignores the opposition and goes straight to the door of the key squares b6, c6 and d6. If you can get in without it, get in. Take the opposition when it is the only way through.
step.t_capablanca: Locked pawns on both sides and the kings far apart. Whoever reaches an enemy pawn first wins. Think: which white king move makes sure of getting there first?
step.t_capablanca.hint1: Count the squares between the kings on the e-file. With an even number, the side to move can take the opposition.
step.capablanca: Now the example Capablanca chose to show the value of the opposition, in Chess Fundamentals. Each side has two blocked pawns, b4 against b5 and h4 against h5, and the kings are on e1 and e8, with six squares between them. An even number: whoever is to move takes the opposition, and whoever takes the opposition wins, because he reaches the other side's pawn first. Ke2 is the only move that wins. Kd1 and Kf1 lose, and Kd2 and Kf2 only draw.
step.capablancaMove: White to play and win. Take the distant opposition and, when the black king leaves the file, do not follow him: step forward on the other side and take the opposition again.
step.capablancaMove.hint: Ke2 first. After ...Kf8, Ke3 would be a mistake: ...Ke7 would follow, with the opposition for Black. Step sideways and forward, Kd3, and wait for the black king to come back to the e-file.
step.capablancaMove.done: Exactly. Ke2, and after ...Kf8 the sidestep Kd3, the mirror image of the Kf3 Capablanca gives against ...Kd8 (Kf2 works too, keeping five squares in between). When the black king came back to e7, Ke3 took the opposition again with three squares in between. From here the white king goes to the b5-pawn or the h5-pawn, whichever Black leaves.
step.defend: The other side of the coin. With a king on e7 against a king on f3 and a pawn on g3, Black to move draws, but in one way only: Kf7, the white king's file with three squares in between. That is distant opposition for the defence. With it, every time the white king comes forward, you face him, and the pawn never gains the tempo it needed.
step.defendMove: Black to play and draw. Take the distant opposition and, when the white king comes up, face him.
step.defendMove.hint: Kf7. If the white king goes to e4, go to e6; if he pushes the pawn, come back to f6.
step.defendMove.done: Perfect. Kf7 from afar, Ke6 face to face, and after g4 the king comes back to f6, a key square of the g4-pawn, and the white king cannot get in. The white king never reaches f5, g5 or h5.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: kings on the same file, rank or diagonal, with one, three or five squares between them and the other side to move, you have the opposition. Second: distant opposition is there to become direct opposition and to get you into a key square; if you can get in without it, get in. Third: when the other king leaves the line, do not follow him sideways; step forward on the other side and take the opposition again. For the defender, the mirror image: take the opposition from afar and face every advance.
step.finish: Now play until you queen. The kings are not on the same line: find the square that takes the distant opposition, turn it into direct opposition and take the king to a key square.
ex.e09: White to play and win. The black king stands in front of the key squares and yours is in the corner.
ex.e09.hint: First the black king's file, from afar. Then, every time he moves, shorten the distance facing him.
ex.e09.solution: Kg2! takes the distant opposition on the g-file, with five squares in between. After ...Kf7, Kf3!; after ...Ke6, Ke4!; and after ...Kd6, Kd4! Every step keeps the number odd, down to direct opposition beside the pawn. Starting with the pawn or with another king move draws.
ex.e11: Black to play and draw. The white pawn is still on the second rank, and the white king is far away. Only one move holds.
ex.e11.hint: The white king is on e1. Get onto his file and, with every step he takes, face him, even if he changes file.
ex.e11.solution: Ke7! Kings on e1 and e7, five squares between them, White to move: the distant opposition is yours. After Kd2, Kd6!, with three squares between; after Kd3, Kd5!, face to face; and after Kc3, Kc5! The white king never reaches the key squares of the c2-pawn, b4, c4 and d4. Any other first move lets the white king take the opposition, and at every step of the defence only one move holds.
ex.e13: White to play and draw. Black has two pawns against one, and the black king wants to come in along the second rank to win the e3-pawn. Only one move holds.
ex.e13.hint: The kings are on the same rank. The opposition also works sideways and from afar: count the squares between them.
ex.e13.solution: Kg1! Kings on c1 and g1, three squares between them, d1, e1 and f1, and Black to move: the distant opposition along the rank is yours. After ...Kd2, Kf2!, side by side with one square between; after ...Kd3, Kf3! The black king never sets foot on e2 or e4, and the e3-pawn stays. Kf2? looks more active, but after ...Kd2 it is your move and Black has the opposition; Kf1? loses to ...Kd1!. A position from Moorthattil's Distant Opposition study on Lichess.
ex.e14: A study by Nikolai Grigoriev, 1933. White to play and win. Black keeps a pawn move in reserve to pass the move.
ex.e14.hint: With the black king on b4, you want yours on b2 with Black to move. Going to b2 at once gives Black the chance to answer with the pawn. Stay one step away from b2.
ex.e14.solution: Ka1!! Kb2? is already direct opposition against the king on b4, but ...d4! passes the move, and you are the one who has to give way. From a1, if ...d4, Kb2! and the opposition belongs to White. After ...Kc3, Kb1!; after ...Kb4, Kc1 (a1 and a2 also do); after ...Kc3, Kd1! (or Kb1). When the pawn finally advances, ...d4 Kc1 d3 cxd3 Kxd3, your king goes to b2, in front of the b3-pawn, and wins. On the first move, Kb1, Kb2, c3+ and c4 only draw.
ex.e15: A study by Nikolai Grigoriev, 1932. White to play and win. The black king wants to get back to the queenside and win your pawns.
ex.e15.hint: The kings will climb side by side, each on its own file. Your pawns hold waiting moves: spend each one only when it passes the move at the right moment.
ex.e15.solution: Kg4!, and after ...Ke3, c3!: the pawn leaves the black king's reach and keeps its second step, c4, for later. The kings climb side by side, Kg5 ...Ke5, Kg6 ...Ke6, Kg7 ...Ke7, with one square between them and White to move: the opposition along the rank is Black's. But on the seventh rank the black king has nowhere higher to go, and c4! passes the move (stepping back with Kg6 also wins, but only postpones the decision). After ...Ke6, Kf8! and Ke7 go round the black king and reach the c5-pawn first. On the first move, c3 allows ...Kf3 with the opposition for Black; on the second, c4 lets the black king come back.
ex.e16: A study by Nikolai Grigoriev, 1929. White to play and draw. The kings are on the same file, with six squares between them.
ex.e16.hint: Ke2 would take the distant opposition, but the fight is not on the e-file: the black king will go round by the queenside to the e5-pawn. Think about your king's target and which square it must be on when the black king reaches e5.
ex.e16.solution: Kf2!! Ke2? takes the opposition and loses: ...Kd7!, ...Kc6, ...Kb5, and the black king goes round. h6? loses to ...Kf7. The white king's target is the h7-pawn: after ...Kd7, h6! fixes it, and the king heads for the kingside, always in step with the black king: ...Kc6 Kg3!, ...Kd5 Kh4!, ...Kd4 Kh5!, ...Ke4 Kg4!, ...Kxe5 Kg5! In the last two moves the kings stand on the same rank, side by side, with one square between them and Black to move: the black king gives way, and the white one reaches f6 and the h7-pawn. If 1...Ke7, Kf3!!, for the same reason. Every white move in the line is the only one that draws.
key.lesson: The lesson position: king on d3 against king on e8, pawn on g3. Ke4! takes the distant opposition, Kf5! and Kg5! turn it into direct opposition and the key square. Own position.
key.diagonal: Diagonal opposition: king on f3 against king on d6, pawn on e3. Kf4! enters the diagonal; Ke4! turns it into direct opposition; Kf5 enters the key square. Own position.
key.means: A means to an end: Ke4 takes the opposition and only draws; Kc5! goes straight to the door of the key squares. A chapter of arex's Lichess Practice; the remark is Averbakh's, via Wikipedia.
key.capablanca: Capablanca's example in Chess Fundamentals: whoever is to move wins. Ke2! takes the distant opposition; after ...Kf8, the sidestep Kd3! Kd1 and Kf1 lose.
key.wikiDiagonal: From Wikipedia: Black to move. White has direct opposition, but it is no use; after ...Kf8, Kd6! takes diagonal opposition and, after ...Ke8, Ke6 the direct one, on a square that matters.
key.studyDefence: From Lichess Practice: White to play and draw. Kf1! takes the distant opposition on the black king's file; Kg2? loses to ...Kg4.
history: The opposition is as old as the study of pawn endings, but it was José Raúl Capablanca who explained it to the ordinary player. In Chess Fundamentals, from 1921, he gives it a whole chapter, shows its three forms, frontal, diagonal and lateral, and tells the student to move the kings apart along the same line to discover distant opposition. His rule fits in one sentence: kings on the same line with an even number of squares between them, the player to move has the opposition; with an odd number, the player who has just moved. His example with two blocked pawns on each side, where whoever is to move wins, is today the distant-opposition diagram on Wikipedia and a chapter of Lichess Practice. Averbakh, decades later, added the warning that closes this lesson: the opposition is a means, and the end is the key square.
practice: Now the real ending: king on h3, pawn on f3, and the black king on e6, in front of the key squares. Find the diagonal, turn it into direct opposition and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
